prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength to reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: Having read the eight opening ballots, I move B040 from second to first in my own ordering. It is the only entry that six of eight members placed in their top three, and the support comes from members with very different backgrounds (atomic physics, condensed matter, statistical physics, electron microscopy and astroparticle physics), which suggests the case does not depend on one subfield's taste. The scientific case is a single clear invention: the magic-wavelength lattice lets a large ensemble of neutral atoms be interrogated at optical frequencies without a trap-induced shift of the clock transition, and the platform has been taken to the 1e-18 regime. It is reproduced and compared across many laboratories, underpins the prospective redefinition of the second, and has opened relativistic geodesy and constraints on fundamental constants and ultralight fields. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and first strontium demonstrations, Ye for the accuracy and stability frontier, a natural two-person prize that does not force an arbitrary cut within a collaboration. From an instrument builder's perspective this is exactly the kind of achievement where the measurement capability is the discovery.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness from earlier precision-measurement prizes: the 2005 prize (Hall, Haensch) covered the optical frequency comb on which every optical clock depends, and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) honoured control of single quantum systems, including the ion-clock lineage. A citation that reads as a refinement of those would be weak. A second concern is that part of the impact is prospective, since the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Finally, the credit to Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow and the wider JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE community is real, and a two-name prize necessarily simplifies a field with several strong groups.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B040 first as an advance in what can be measured and how accurately, and flags whether it is sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
responses.response: I agree with the ranking and take his distinctness worry seriously rather than dismissing it. My view is that the distinction is real: the comb is a ruler, and the 2012 work controlled single quantum objects, whereas the lattice clock solved a different problem, namely how to combine the signal-to-noise of thousands of atoms with the absence of motional and trap shifts. That is a conceptual step (the magic wavelength) rather than a refinement, and the citation should name it explicitly. I would, however, not rest the case on the metrology redefinition, which is still pending.

responses.point: Lindroth sees a clear, concrete, high-impact discovery with a single coherent story, and ranks B032 (trapped-ion logic with Cirac, Zoller and Blatt) second.
responses.response: I share her reading of B040, but I differ on B032 as a companion or substitute. The ion-trap gate idea is foundational, yet it overlaps with B004 and with Zoller's role there, the experimental credit beyond Blatt (Wineland, Monroe) cannot be accommodated within three names, and the 2012 and 2025 prizes already cover neighbouring ground. I would keep B032 below B040 until the committee can argue how a prize would avoid being read as a duplicate of 2012.

responses.point: Danielsson puts B023 (precision CMB mapping) first and B035 second, and ranks IceCube third, arguing that the CMB and Higgs results are mature and complete.
responses.response: I accept that B023 is mature, but I would qualify it: COBE (2006) and Peebles (2019) already cover much of this territory, and the five names supplied cannot be reduced to three without excluding Puget or Sunyaev, whose claims he himself calls strong. As for B035, I agree on the importance, yet the Higgs attribution problem across ATLAS and CMS remains unsolved, and I would not recommend a prize whose laureate list the committee must defend as arbitrary. I do agree with him that IceCube is a clean new-messenger discovery, which is why I keep B018 as an alternative even though I have moved it down.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first but concedes that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits overlaps and that credit among theorists and experimentalists is unsettled; she also flags her own institutional proximity.
responses.response: I appreciate the candid conflict disclosure, and I think the overlap issue is serious: a cQED prize so soon after 2025 would need an argument that it is a distinct discovery rather than the technological consequence of the circuit work already honoured. I would therefore not put B055 in front of B040 this year. I would be glad to hear her case for why strong coupling in circuits is distinct, since it is her field.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the KPZ entry B005 first and Cirac and Zoller's B004 second, rating B040 third, and notes that the clock's measurement impact is partly prospective since the second has not been redefined.
responses.response: His prospective-impact point is fair and I have included it in my own reservation. I do not think it is decisive: the 1e-18 performance, the international comparisons and the geodesy and fundamental-constant tests are already realised, so the prospective part is an application, not a doubt about the discovery. On B005, I find the physics beautiful, but it was ranked highly by him alone, with a single experimental confirmation in the flagship liquid-crystal system and missing credit for the exact solutions; I do not see the committee support to carry it, and I would like to hear whether he thinks the exact-solution contributors can be reconciled with a three-name limit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the optical lattice clock is a distinct achievement from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-ion control prizes
Whether the citation can name the magic-wavelength lattice concept without understating the contributions of other clock groups
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing
Whether IceCube (B018) with only Halzen and Karle, or a three-name Higgs allocation (B035), would be judged more defensible if B040 stalls
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented personal or institutional tie to the optical-clock community, so no specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B040. For the record, my profile documents PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur connections and a CERN doctoral background, which touch the astroparticle field of B018 and the detector collaboration world of B035; no specific link to the IceCube, ATLAS or CMS collaborations is documented, but I would flag that proximity if either became the leading option.
